papers.title: Marker direction and donor structure alter genetic cell-stateprioritization in endometriosis: convergent evidence from single-cell chromatin
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify regions of the genome linked to disease, but they do not tell us which cells are involved. Researchers often address that question by testing marker genes from single-cell atlases. We asked how much the answer changes when those markers are defined differently. Reconstructing a published endometriosis analysis, we found that selecting genes with large fold changes in either direction prioritized venous endothelium, whereas selecting up-regulated genes prioritized decidual stroma (the latter was not significant after within-family false-discovery correction). A calibrated benchmark, six-trait control panel, and donor-level checks showed why neither rule can be trusted on its own. In an independent RNA atlas, stromal programs were repeatedly prioritized, although closely related perivascular states remained plausible. We then examined an independent molecular layer: chromatin accessibility in 36,073 nuclei from 12 endometrial biopsies. The initially specified analysis found enrichment of endometriosis heritability in stromal accessible chromatin (z = 4.11, one-sided p = 2 x 10^-5). In a later, more stringent joint model with baselineLD v2.2, the stromal coefficient remained positive (z = 3.83, p = 6.47 x 10^-5) and exceeded the epithelial coefficient (z = 3.68, p = 1.18 x 10^-4). Both effects remained nominally significant when each biopsy was excluded in turn (12/12 analyses). The association was also seen for leiomyoma, and the endometriosis GWAS share participants. Together, these findings support a broad stromal regulatory context for part of inherited endometriosis risk, but do not establish a unique causal cell state or a lesion cell of origin.

papers.title: MeXalign - A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
papers.abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality.

papers.title: One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS): statistical analysis and interpretation of quantitative proteomics data for non-coders
papers.abstract: Open-source statistical methods for proteomic differential abundance analysis are well established. Normalization, missing-value handling, and the statistical model must suit the experimental design and change how proteins are called. Together with the frequent need for data reformatting, coding and bioinformatics expertise, these elements limit the bench scientist's analysis of datasets. Here, we present One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS), a no-code R Shiny application that parses Proteome Discoverer, MaxQuant, FragPipe, DIA-NN or Spectronaut search results for user-driven interactive exploration through transformation and differential analysis. Upon import, OSMSS records the experimental design through user questions, selects the analysis workflow, identifies normalization requirements, runs established statistical methods, and records every analytical step in a case-specific methods text. OSMSS supports label-free data-dependent and data-independent acquisition (DDA, DIA) and tandem mass tag (TMT) group comparisons, affinity-purification comparisons, and DIA and TMT phosphosite analyses. OSMSS runs on local devices or servers and provides volcano plots, heatmaps, trend analysis, kinase prediction, pathway enrichment and kinase activity inference. In seven benchmarks, OSMSS performed comparably to matched reference workflows. OSMSS lets bench scientists apply established statistical models and associated tools transparently and without coding, enabling a more informed analysis of their data.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Mucosal Luminal Interface Metaproteomics Reveals Diagnostic Potential of Microbial Proteins in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Abstract: Background: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with two main subtypes, Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC), is associated with more aggressive phenotypes and greater diagnostic complexity in pediatric patients. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, lack sufficient distinguishing power between IBD subtypes. This study aimed to investigate and compare proteomic and metaproteomic profiles of pediatric IBD (PIBD) patients and healthy controls to develop a diagnostic panel capable of accurately diagnose IBD and distinguish its subtypes. Methods: We performed an in-depth evaluation of mucosal luminal interface samples from PIBD patients and healthy individuals, separately analyzing both the human proteome and microbial metaproteome data. The study involved selecting appropriate protein sets, employing feature selection techniques and machine learning across three intestinal regions: the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and descending colon. Results: Notably, panels composed solely of microbial biomarkers outperformed both human-only and combined human-microbial panels, achieving highly accurate results. Furthermore, the ascending colon emerged as the optimal sampling site, a result that aligns with the rich microbial diversity revealed in its taxonomic profile. Conclusions: Using a machine learning-based strategy on combined proteomics and metaproteomics, this study uncovered disease-relevant signaling pathways and delivered taxonomic as well as functional insights into the microbial dysbiosis of PIBD. A diagnostic panel built around microbial proteins (particularly those originating from the ascending colon) emerges as a promising tool for more precise stratification of PIBD subtypes. Larger, prospective studies are now needed to validate these candidate biomarkers and translate them into clinically deployable diagnostic panels. Keywords: Metaproteome, Biomarker, Pediatric Inflammatory bowel disease, Machine learning, Mucosal luminal interface.

papers.title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics resolves gene expression in physical space, but the spatial statistics typically used to quantify spatial organization scale poorly to imaging-based datasets with hundreds-of-thousands of cells and thousands of genes. We recast the standard spatial-autocorrelation statistics as convolutions on a rasterized representation of the gene expression matrix and evaluate them with the fast Fourier transform. Measuring spatial statistics across multiple length scales becomes tractable for every gene using this approach, which extends naturally to differential reorganization testing between two tissue conditions.

papers.title: PlantTV: a versatile user-friendly software to explore RNA-seq data across plant species
papers.abstract: Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become a central tool in plant biology for studying genome-wide transcriptional responses. However, interpretation of differential expression results remains challenging, particularly for non-model species where functional annotation resources are fragmented, heterogeneous, or incomplete. Existing user-friendly RNA-seq analysis platforms often rely on predefined annotation databases, limiting their applicability across the diversity of plant species. We developed Plant Transcriptomics Viewer (PlantTV), a free web-based platform for interactive exploration of plant RNA-seq datasets. PlantTV integrates differential expression analysis, expression visualization, functional enrichment analysis, and co-expression network exploration within a single graphical interface. A central feature is the Annotation Builder, which allows users to generate reusable annotation tables from diverse resources, including GFF/GTF files, EggNOG annotations, BLAST results, and custom tabular datasets. Using case studies in Arabidopsis thaliana, Malus domestica, and Eucalyptus melliodora, we demonstrate that PlantTV supports transcriptome analysis across a range of annotation scenarios, from well-annotated reference genomes to de novo transcriptome assemblies. PlantTV provides an interactive and species-independent environment for plant transcriptome analysis. By combining RNA-seq exploration tools with flexible support for custom annotation resources, PlantTV facilitates biological interpretation of transcriptomic datasets in both model and non-model plant species.

papers.title: A session-aware test protocol, energy-based strand pairing and a measured crossing-resolution limit for automated DNA knot identification in atomic force microscopy images
papers.abstract: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) resolves the crossings of single knotted and linked DNA molecules, so the knot type can in principle be read from one image. TopoStats, to our knowledge the only automated pipeline for this task, assigns the correct type to fewer than 8% of the knots and catenanes in a public dataset of 721 molecules imaged in 20 sessions. Image classifiers appear to do better, but 18 of the 20 sessions contain a single knot type, so a classifier can score well by recognizing the session. We present three tools for evaluating and tracing these molecules. First, a session-aware protocol holds out whole imaging sessions, scores only the four classes not separable by size, and uses a probe to test whether images identify their session. Three classifiers reached 58-67% balanced accuracy on knots on their training sessions but only 27-32% under this protocol, near the 25% chance level, and the probe identified the session above chance in all eight tests. Second, an energy-based method connects strands through crossings by DNA length and stiffness. It traced the loops of 84% of knots and catenanes correctly, compared with 32% for TopoStats. Third, we measured the crossing-resolution limit of the pipeline. Labels derived from the known handedness of the knots gave the correct upper strand at 173 crossings without manual annotation, and the existing width rule ordered 137 of them (79%) correctly. A convolutional network did not exceed it. With the new pairing, the knot type was still correct for only 6-8% of knots and catenanes, because 72% of those with a valid pairing had lost crossings when closely spaced crossings were merged. Classifiers for AFM images should therefore be tested on new sessions, and further progress depends on resolving dense crossings. The protocol, labels and code are openly available.

papers.title: AptaRender: an interactive drawing and styling tool for 2D nucleic acid structures
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) diagrams are widely used to communicate nucleic acid secondary structure, yet the path from a sequence and pairing model to an editable publication figure often requires either specialized software or substantial cleanup in a general-purpose graphics editor. AptaRender (v2.3.1, available at https://yjhe99.github.io/aptarender/) is a browser-based editor that converts a set of user-supplied DNA or RNA sequences and their dot-bracket structures into an interactive 2D drawing. The software separates structure specification from visual composition: it does not predict folding, but provides direct control over the layout, nucleotide styling, base pair styling, numbering and export. AptaRender supports simultaneously working with multiple sequences, customized per-nucleotide sizing and coloring with customized styles, manual branching and motif repositioning, constrained rotation of helices around loop rings, and visualization of a user defined hybridization region between two strands. Drawings are exported as editable SVG or high-resolution PNG. The application is implemented as a single dependency-free HTML file that runs entirely in the browser and stores working state locally. This design makes the tool easy to distribute and suitable for rapid preparation of figures for manuscripts, presentations, and exploratory communication. AptaRender complements prediction and template-based visualization software by concentrating on lightweight, local, art directed figure construction. Across eight test cases, AptaRender reliably generated accurate, information-rich 2D nucleic acid structures and exported them in PNG and SVG formats, although specialized annotations and additional symbols required external editing.

papers.title: An apicomplexan-specific foundation model improves prediction of regulatory genomic signals in Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn transferable sequence representations through self-supervision, yet their practical value is contested. In data-rich mammalian genomes, task-specific models trained from scratch can match or exceed pretrained models on many regulatory prediction tasks. Whether self-supervised pretraining provides an advantage in small, data-sparse genomes has not been directly tested. We address this in the compact, 23Mbp, A/T-rich genome of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. We trained a Genomic Pretrained Network (GPN) via masked-nucleotide reconstruction on 455 genome assemblies spanning 76 apicomplexan species. We then fine-tuned the model to predict a variety of epigenomic features in a held-out chromosome, including transcription factor binding sites, chromatin-accessibility, histone modifications, and 10 chromatin states. Pretraining followed by fine tuning improved prediction of most features, with most of the benefit concentrated on datasets with relatively little labeled data (fewer than 3,000 training examples). In contrast, a human-pretrained model transferred poorly, indicating that phylogenetically relevant pretraining, not foundation-model status alone, drives beneficial performance. Self-supervised pretraining on clade-specific assemblies is thus a practical route to data-efficient regulatory modeling in small genomes where training data is scarce.

papers.title: Integrating Unsupervised Clustering with Transformer-Based Models for De Novo Cell Population Identification
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing has been widely applied across the life sciences. It enables accurate and robust identification of cell types in heterogeneous biological tissues through unsupervised clustering, shallow learning, and deep learning. While deep learning does not outperform shallow learning in classification performance, it streamlines cell type identification by eliminating cumbersome preprocessing procedures. However, the availability of training datasets with comprehensive cell type annotations is always limited, so new datasets inevitably contain cell populations that are not pre-defined in the training data. To address this limitation, we integrated unsupervised clustering with transformer-based models to identify cell populations unrecognized by classical methods. Specifically, we developed the Nankai GeneRank Classifier by fine-tuning the pre-trained Geneformer-V1 model, and then clustered cells based on its softmax-normalized class probability matrix (SCPM). Applied to a public colorectal cancer dataset, the new method, named SCPM-based clustering, resolved cell populations that cannot be unambiguously identified by classical methods alone and led to the discovery of novel candidate markers of colorectal cancer stem cells, demonstrating its utility.

papers.title: Survival-informed mutational network clustering reveals prognostic glioma architectures
papers.abstract: Cancer heterogeneity remains a major challenge for predicting patient outcomes. To address this challenge, we introduce SNOWS (Survival-iNfOrmed netWork cluStering), a probabilistic framework that integrates somatic mutations, clinical covariates and survival information to discover patient groups with distinct mutation patterns and survival profiles, using Bayesian networks to capture dependencies involving mutations and clinical variables. Applied to 950 adult-type diffuse gliomas from TCGA, SNOWS identified three clusters that transferred successfully to classify an independent CGGA cohort of 181 patients using mutation and clinical data, without requiring their survival outcomes. The transferred clusters showed distinct survival, mutation profiles and dependency structures, and provided prognostic information beyond WHO 2021 tumour subtype, age and sex, significantly increasing the C-index from 0.691 to 0.712. Cluster assignments were driven by specific mutation frequencies, with network dependencies improving the assignments of patients with less typical molecular profiles. Beyond glioma, SNOWS also improved prognostic discrimination in pan-kidney and pan-myeloid cohorts. These results support survival-informed network clustering as a general framework for resolving clinically relevant cancer heterogeneity.

papers.title: OrthoSimulator: Empirically trained simulations for ground-truth benchmarking of orthology inference
papers.abstract: Orthology inference is foundational for comparative genomics, enabling the reconstruction of phylogenetic relationships and transfer of biological knowledge between species. Methods often infer different orthogroups and orthologous relationships, making robust benchmarking essential for evaluating their accuracy. Existing resources such as the Quest for Orthologs benchmark service and OrthoBench provide valuable benchmarks grounded in real biological data and expert curation. However, the true evolutionary histories in all of these benchmarks are unknown, and therefore the true accuracy of orthology inference methods is unknown. Simulations provide an approach to evaluate accuracy where the complete ground truth is known. However, simulations are only useful for benchmarking if they realistically reflect empirical data. Here, we introduce OrthoSimulator, a Python package for generating realistic, empirically calibrated benchmark datasets with known orthogroups, orthologous relationships, gene trees, and evolutionary events. We demonstrate its utility by benchmarking widely used orthology inference methods across simulations calibrated from multiple methods and empirical datasets. We show that method-to-method variability in ortholog inference accuracy is robust to variation in simulation parameters. We further provide a detailed evaluation of ortholog inference accuracy through independent cross-validation, and show that OrthoFinder is the most accurate of the four methods tested. OrthoSimulator is freely available at https://github.com/lauriebelch/OrthoSimulator.

papers.title: Joint Analysis of Common Regulatory and Rare Coding Variants for Improved Power in Kernel Association Tests
papers.abstract: Rare alleles arise from mutations on an existing haplotype background, yet current gene-based rare variant association tests treat low-frequency coding variants as effects independent of the common regulatory variants that surround them. The penetrance of rare coding variants can be modulated by the cis-regulatory landscape, and failing to account for this context limits the statistical power of existing methods for complex traits. We present PrediXSKAT, a kernel-based rare variant association framework that incorporates the surrounding cis-regulatory landscape by estimating its impact on gene expression via PrediXcan. PrediXSKAT embeds predicted gene expression directly into the Sequence Kernel Association Test kernel through element-wise similarity weighting, concentrating rare variant signal among individuals who share concordant genetic and regulatory backgrounds. Comprehensive simulations demonstrate that PrediXSKAT increases power over standard kernel-based testing under biologically realistic conditions where a proportion of tested variants carry small, mixed-direction effects. Type I error rates are controlled in the absence of association. Power gains persist across a range of sample sizes and causal variant architectures. Applied to whole-genome sequencing data from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, PrediXSKAT recapitulates established disease loci and amplifies signals at previously unreported candidate genes without indiscriminately inflating genome-wide results. PrediXSKAT provides a generalizable and extensible framework for the joint analysis of common regulatory and rare coding variants. The approach can be applied to any kernel-based set test and extended to jointly consider multiple genes within the same biological pathway, offering a principled strategy for improving rare variant discovery in large-scale sequencing studies of complex disease.

papers.title: Point mutations in the FimH lectin domain: predicted folding stability versus conformational dynamics for R60P, Q133K and Y137A
papers.abstract: Background. The adhesin FimH attaches uropathogenic Escherichia coli to the urinary epithelium through a force-regulated catch-bond that single lectin-domain substitutions can modulate. How such substitutions reshape the dynamics of the isolated lectin domain, and whether stability predictors anticipate them, is unclear. Methods. We compared the wild-type (WT) lectin domain (PDB 4XO8, apo) with R60P, Y137A and Q133K, using three 500 ns molecular dynamics (MD) replicates per system (6 microseconds total) and three folding-stability predictors (FoldX, a Cartesian-ddG-type Rosetta protocol, ERIS-2). The replicate was the unit of analysis (n = 3), with 95% confidence intervals and a WT replicate-to-replicate control. Results. FoldX and ERIS-2 ranked the variants consistently, R60P most destabilising and Q133K neutral; the Rosetta value for Q133K was anomalously high. All systems stayed folded. R60P gave the only reproduced local change, loss of beta-strand structure at residues 60-61 and of three local hydrogen bonds. Y137A did not bring Thr158 into the pocket, and the Q133K Gln133-Asp54 polar contact became a Lys133-Asp54 salt bridge. In the principal-component landscape, departures from the WT region came from individual replicates (Y137A replicate 1; Q133K replicates 2-3), not a systematic shift. Conclusions. A substitution perturbs local structure most clearly when it breaks a beta-strand (R60P), and the stability predictions and dynamics together give a consistent ranking of the variants, including the first dynamic characterisation of Q133K. The results characterise the apo lectin domain and give a reproducible basis for interpreting FimH mutations, not for inferring affinity. Keywords: FimH; lectin domain; point mutations; molecular dynamics; folding stability ({Delta}{Delta}G); protein stability prediction; principal component analysis; urinary tract infection.

papers.title: DNA methylation assigns sequencing reads to closely related bacterial strains when their sequence cannot
papers.abstract: Clinical and public-health questions often concern strains rather than species, yet co-resident strains of one species can be so closely related that a single long read carries no sequence difference between them. We measured how often this happens in 639 pairs of isolates of Enterococcus faecium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus sequenced on one nanopore platform. Among the 297 pairs above 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI), 40.37% of read placements (a read counted against one strain's genome) carried no sequence difference between the two strains, and above 99.9% ANI about three quarters did. Strains of one species also differ in the DNA motifs they methylate. Our method, Epilect, assigns single nanopore reads to strains from the basecaller's methylation calls, given a methylation profile for each strain, and declines to call when the evidence is weak. In the pairs above 99% ANI it correctly assigned 21.8% of the read placements that sequence could not place, at a precision of 0.959. In computational mixtures of 65 pairs of distinct strains at or above 99.5% ANI that were predicted to differ in methylation, its per-read F1 score exceeded that of the best of three sequence-based read-phasing tools by 0.25 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.37); where equally related strains were predicted to share a methylome, the comparison reversed. DNA methylation therefore supplies strain evidence on reads whose sequence carries none, and whether it will do so for a given pair of strains can be estimated before sequencing.

papers.title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

papers.title: From Screening to Differential Diagnosis: Benchmarking 3D Facial Representations Across Craniofacial Conditions
papers.abstract: Rare genetic disorders often present with highly heterogeneous physical features: some have distinctive craniofacial characteristics, whereas others produce subtler or more variable facial differences, making phenotype-based diagnosis challenging. Three-dimensional (3D) facial scanning is a noninvasive approach that captures facial shape and surface geometry, providing quantitative information on craniofacial morphology beyond conventional 2D photographs. Here, we investigated how well 3D facial representations support clinical tasks ranging from broad screening to fine-grained differential diagnosis without landmark registration, dense correspondence, or template fitting. We benchmarked four 3D models, including PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, and a geometric baseline, using 26,990 facial scans from 18,785 subjects across four prediction tasks. Across models, performance declined as greater diagnostic specificity was required. Broad affected-versus-unaffected screening achieved high performance (accuracy 0.893; AUC 0.956), although sensitivity analyses revealed substantial influences of cohort composition and demographic differences. Fine-grained syndrome diagnosis remained more challenging, with limited top-1 accuracy despite meaningful class-wise discrimination. Combining repeated scans improved patient-level diagnosis beyond differences in patient weighting. Prototype inference further improved diagnostic prioritization, placing the correct syndrome among the top five candidates for about 65% of held-out patients across 49 diagnoses. Patient-to-patient retrieval identified phenotypically similar confirmed cases, while useful syndrome prototypes could be constructed from relatively few reference patients. Anatomical region-occlusion analysis revealed syndrome-dependent patterns of facial importance broadly consistent with clinically recognized craniofacial features, although overlapping facial phenotypes contributed to diagnostic confusion. Overall, these findings support the potential of 3D facial representations for diagnostic candidate prioritization and retrieval, while emphasizing the influence of cohort composition on screening performance and the challenges of distinguishing phenotypically similar genetic syndromes.

papers.title: Algorithms for Designing Therapeutic Oligonucleotides on Pangenome Graphs
papers.abstract: Designing therapeutic oligonucleotides that act reliably across human genetic diversity requires more than alignment to a single reference genome. Binding affinity of an siRNA or ASO to a usually complementary site in an mRNA target molecule is one main determinant of drug efficacy. Thus, variation in sub-populations can lead to failures in drug development if this variation reduces binding affinity. We provide a first methodological step towards principled, variant-aware design of therapeutic oligonucleotides. The genetic diversity in target genes, or specific regions thereof, is represented as a pangenome graph. We define individual or small sets of suitable therapeutic oligonucleotides by their ability to cover all paths in a directed acyclic graph within a bounded edit distance <= k. Edit distance is used as an accepted proxy to the commonly used binding affinity. We formalize the resulting computational problem and provide complexity results: NP-hardness of identifying such minimal sets even for k =0, and coNP-completeness of verifying the validity of a given set of oligonucleotides. Further, we propose algorithmic approaches operating on a product graph of an automaton (an Aho-Corasick DFA or an Ukkonen DFA) and the pangenome graph, as well as a dynamic programming-based lossless filter. We evaluate the approaches on gene-specific subgraphs of human pangenome graphs and demonstrate favorable performance compared to naive brute-force computation. Our results show that candidate target sites with a threshold of k <= 3 can be identified even for large, complex graphs where the brute-force computation did not complete within 24h. We observe that the dynamic programming-based lossless filter outperforms both product-graph approaches as well as brute-force baselines while maintaining an average approximation ratio < 1.5 across more than a hundred evaluated subgraphs. We also present examples where a small set of oligonucleotides constitutes a feasible solution where no single oligonucleotide with a threshold of k <= 2 covers all paths.

papers.title: Chimera: Cross-Species Single-Cell Generative Modeling of Expression Deployment Relative to Protein Conservation
papers.abstract: A protein's sequence says what a gene could do in another species; the cells of that species say what it does there. Comparative genomics measures the first. Chimera measures the second, a gene's deployment, on the same genes and reports the difference. It aligns single-cell atlases across species in one generative model and returns, for every one-to-one ortholog, the evidence in the counts for a shared expression pattern, and {Delta}[a], the position of that evidence above or below what the protein's identity predicts. This difference is not sequence constraint under another name: across eight tissues, protein identity tracks dN/dS, whereas {Delta}[a] tracks neither. A gene therefore has two coordinates, not one, and the second can contradict the first: spermatocyte genes such as ZPBP2 keep their stage pattern on less conserved proteins, in eight held-out species, whereas conserved hepatocyte enzymes such as ALAS1 share their pattern but not their level. More broadly, genes of specialized cells sit above what their proteins predict in 23 of 24 cohorts, and approved drug targets do so more often than matched genes. Even among nearly identical proteins, where sequence can no longer tell genes apart, the count evidence still does. Nor does this rest on the model alone: independent data support the count evidence in liver and testis and, in a pre-specified test, {Delta}[a] in liver. With both coordinates, one can ask whether another species uses a gene as humans do, the premise of every animal model of a disease gene or drug target.

papers.title: Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments reveal modular architecture and expand functional coverage in bacteriophage proteins
papers.abstract: Bacteriophage proteins evolve through extensive modular exchange, yet the sequence units underlying this process remain poorly defined. Classical domains are plausible evolutionary modules, but they incompletely annotate phage proteins and may not always coincide with the regions conserved across protein families. Here, we constructed 13,035 Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments (ECFs), grouped into 3,167 families, through large-scale HMM-HMM comparisons of proteins from 5,396 RefSeq phage genomes, without imposing predefined domain boundaries. ECFs overlapped substantially with ECOD and Pfam annotations but formed a heterogeneous spectrum comprising subdomains, domain-equivalent units, composite regions and fragments with no counterpart in either resource. Their relationships were frequently nested, indicating that conserved modules occur at multiple organisational scales. ECFs annotated 50% of phage representative proteins (at least doubling the coverage of either database), with the largest gains in structural and infection-related functions, a pattern replicated in independent metagenomic data. ECF families also showed function-dependent patterns of diversity and spatial segregation and provided functional associations for 23,925 protein families lacking detectable Pfam or ECOD domains. In receptor-binding proteins, ECFs subdivided established domains, delineated previously unannotated structural elements and recovered homologous regions where structural similarity was ambiguous. These results show that the evolutionary building blocks of phage proteins do not always coincide with classical domains, highlighting that evolutionary processes act across multiple scales. ECFs provide a complementary, sequence-derived framework for investigating how complex viral proteins are assembled, diversified and functionally organised.

papers.title: ECMExplainer: a functional matrisome framework for decoding cellular stress states and aging trajectories
papers.abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as both a hallmark of aging and a durable record of the cellular stress states that shape age-related tissue dysfunction. Despite its apparent role in aging and disease, translating matrisome gene expression into interpretable biological meaning remains an unresolved challenge. Here we introduce ECMExplainer, a framework that uses 180 matrisome gene-pair ratios, partitioned into 76 Assembly/Destruction and 104 Signaling/Signaling pairs to position fibroblast transcriptomes within a functional matrisome phenotype space defined by six reference fibroblast states spanning physiological and stress-associated conditions: Proliferating, Quiescence, Senescence, Fibrosis, Inflammation, and Hypoxia. Because each ratio records only which of the two genes is more highly expressed, it is largely insensitive to sequencing depth and batch offsets, allowing ECMExplainer to outperform magnitude-based classifiers on unseen data. Rather than assigning only a single phenotype label, ECMExplainer measures a sample's coordinate distance to each reference state, enabling quantitative mapping of matrisome state trajectories while giving biological meaning even to conditions that fall between or outside the training phenotypes. Across 20 independent fibroblast datasets, ECMExplainer uncovered conserved ECM signatures underlying diverse fibroblast states and showed that they capture multiple aging-related processes. Specifically, it identified FST/ITGA1 as a rapamycin-sensitive senescence-associated ratio, revealed a fibrosis-biased ECM trajectory in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome distinct from chronological aging, and distinguished successful from failed OSKM reprogramming using an ECM Aging Score without retraining. Together, these findings establish the matrisome as a compact and biologically interpretable carrier of cellular state information, and ECMExplainer as a quantitative foundation for interpreting aging, fibrosis and rejuvenation through the lens of the ECM.

papers.title: Unsupervised Deep Learning for Cryo-EM/ET Particle Classification
papers.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is widely used to determine protein structures from purified samples. With cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET), it is possible to image thin sections of cells and directly visualize diverse proteins in their native environment. However, separating the massive mixture of different types of proteins inside cells remains challenging, especially without human intervention. In this work, we present an unsupervised deep learning framework for classifying cryo-EM/ET particle images that jointly optimizes for pose and structure through an autoencoder-based multi-stage pipeline. On single-particle cryo-EM datasets, our framework can capture the continuous variation in particle views and separate images of real particles from contamination. Using in silico mixtures of multiple types of proteins, we demonstrated our method's capability of separating the protein classes without supervision. Finally in a real cryo-ET dataset of algal chloroplast, our deep learning model successfully detected the four main protein complexes of photosynthesis on native thylakoid membranes. Taken together, these results demonstrate that our framework offers a scalable, annotation-free solution for robust structural discovery across diverse cryo-EM and cryo-ET applications.

papers.title: HieraPTM: From PTM Site Recognition to Functional Phosphosite Prediction through Hierarchical Context and Protein Mechanics
papers.abstract: Protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate cellular signaling and protein function, making accurate site identification essential for understanding protein regulation. However, PTM site recognition and functional phosphosite prediction are largely modeled independently, limiting the transfer of large-scale recognition knowledge to functional prioritization. Here, we introduce HieraPTM-HieraFuncPhos, a cross-task hierarchical framework that separately models and conditionally integrates transferable PTM recognition representations and function-specific mechanical evidence. HieraPTM integrates local sequence patterns, protein language model representations, and three-dimensional structural information to recognize multiple PTM types. HieraFuncPhos transfers these representations through parameter-efficient adaptation and adaptively retrieves local and distal mechanical evidence conditioned on functional representations. At HSP90AA1 T36 and T115, the model reveals distinct mechanical response patterns consistent with published nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observations, suggesting that the framework not only prioritizes functional phosphosites but also provides biophysically grounded, testable hypotheses regarding site-specific regulation. HieraPTM achieved macro-averaged AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.9237 and 0.8425 across eight PTM tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on severely imbalanced external benchmarks. HieraFuncPhos achieved an AUROC of 0.8274 and an AUPRC of 0.8188, outperforming existing comparison methods. Together, this framework connects PTM site recognition, functional prioritization, and structure-informed hypotheses regarding potential regulatory processes.

papers.title: A statistical framework for identifying candidate genetic interactions from adaptive laboratory evolution data
papers.abstract: Background Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) is widely used to improve microbial fitness under defined selective pressures. Mutations accumulated during ALE may interact epistatically, with the effect of one mutation depending on another. Understanding these interactions can help explain adaptive phenotypes and inform combinatorial strain engineering, but experimentally testing all mutation combinations is impractical. We developed a computational framework that uses gene-pair co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity patterns to identify candidates for experimental investigation of epistasis. Results We applied the framework to a curated compendium of 141 Escherichia coli ALE experiments from ALEdb, using the Fisher exact test and DISCOVER as complementary statistical screens. Testing and multiple-testing correction were performed separately within each experiment, method, and direction (co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity). At a 5% false discovery rate threshold, the Fisher exact test identified 74 significant gene pairs, comprising 36 co-occurrences and 38 mutual exclusivities. DISCOVER identified 5 significant pairs, all for mutual exclusivity and also significant under the Fisher exact test. These shared pairs suggested alternative adaptive routes involving temperature tolerance, glycerol utilization, and associations between RNA polymerase subunit genes. The two methods produced similar expected overlaps for Fisher-significant pairs, but the broader null distributions of DISCOVER yielded larger raw p-values. Of the 69 pairs significant only under the Fisher exact test, 60 arose in experiments with multiple strain labels or involved a gene with only one distinct mutation recorded across all affected endpoints (final samples from lineages evolved in parallel), highlighting the need to examine genetic backgrounds and mutation origins when interpreting the results. Power analysis indicated that the Fisher exact test required 70 independent endpoints for co-occurrence and 215 for mutual exclusivity to achieve 80% power under pre-specified scenarios. We implemented the framework as a reusable Nextflow pipeline that automates statistical screening of ALEdb and user-supplied mutation datasets. Conclusions By combining gene-pair screening with mutation-level interpretation, this reproducible framework narrows the search space for experimental investigation of epistasis and can contribute to combinatorial strain design. The power analysis provides sample-size benchmarks for planning future ALE experiments with adequate power to screen for candidate genetic interactions.

papers.title: Phylospatial optimal transport for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data integration
papers.abstract: The spatial organization of evolving cell populations in tumors influences how they progress and respond to treatment. Spatially resolved transcriptomics data may be used to examine the locations of these diverse cell states in tumor sections. However, these technologies often lack single-cell resolution and instead capture groups of cells in spatial spots, making it difficult to resolve cancer clones. In contrast, dissociated single-cell transcriptomics data are better suited for obtaining cell lineages, but do not capture the locations of the cells in the tissue. Here, we introduce SpOTr, an optimal transport approach that leverages the concordance between the evolutionary tree and the spatial distribution of cancer cells to integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data from tumors. SpOTr combines a spot deconvolution model with Fused Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, in which cells that are close in the tree are drawn to nearby spots. In simulations and in real spatial lineage tracing data, SpOTr recovered the spatial locations of clones better than methods that ignore the tree. In a human colorectal liver metastasis, SpOTr mapped copy number clones from dissociated cells to spatial spots, showing that it successfully maps the evolutionary history of tumors in space.

papers.title: DynamicsPLM: A Dynamics-Enriched Small Protein Language Model for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting how mutations impact protein function and stability remains a key challenge in computational biology. Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

papers.title: Spindle: Scalable Indexing of Spatial-Omics Data for Fast Querying
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has unlocked new avenues for biological discovery by jointly capturing gene expression and spatial context. ST datasets are typically stored as gene expression matrices paired with spatial coordinates, supporting queries based on expression levels at individual locations. However, characterizing how genes vary together requires representations of relationships between genes, such as covariance matrices computed over spatial neighborhoods. These gene--gene co-expression patterns capture coordinated biological variation and can reveal spatially localized gene programs. As datasets grow to atlas scale, efficiently searching for such patterns becomes a central computational bottleneck due to the combination of high dimensionality, extreme sparsity, and variability in gene expression across large numbers of spatial regions. Such searches require repeated access to second-order statistics, motivating a compact, searchable representation of spatial co-expression. We address this problem with Spindle, a platform-agnostic indexing algorithm for efficiently searching spatial gene co-expression patterns. Spindle exploits the approximate block-diagonal structure of gene--gene covariance matrices over spatial regions, in which covariances between blocks are small in magnitude, to selectively store informative components while compactly representing recurring covariance patterns. This yields a compressed yet searchable index suitable for atlas-scale spatial datasets. Across multiple real-world biological datasets (87,000--817,000 cells), Spindle indexes are 113--197 times smaller than the whole covariance matrices. A complete query, including query preprocessing, takes 2.8--28 ms on one CPU core, 5.1--16 times faster than a scan over the whole covariance matrices, and the tiles it returns recover a median of 81% of the exact near neighbors. In breast cancer, the regions retrieved by covariance search closely match the cell-type composition of the query (median cell-type composition difference 0.15, compared with 0.54 for random regions). Spindle supports both partial covariance queries and queries specified as gene lists, as well as retrieval across measurement platforms.

papers.title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
papers.abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88). Its predicted variant effects agree with likely causal caQTLs (Spearman correlation = 0.52) but not with variants associated only through linkage, a traditionally challenging task. Overall, ModBERT establishes a framework for personal-genome language modeling, in which a model reads each individual's genetic and epigenetic sequence rather than a shared reference. This enables in silico dissection of variant and methylation effects on gene regulation and principled prioritization of candidates for experimental validation as population-scale long-read cohorts (e.g., 1KGP and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium) grow.

papers.title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
papers.abstract: Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Characterizing Multimodal Mutational Processes in Cancer Using MOTET
papers.abstract: Mutational signatures are characteristic patterns of somatic alterations in cancer genomes. A single aberrant mechanism can simultaneously generate coordinated patterns of alterations across multiple mutation modalities, including single-base substitutions (SBSs), doublet-base substitutions (DBSs), and small insertions and deletions (IDs). However, these signatures are typically inferred separately and linked post hoc, obscuring their shared underlying mechanisms. To resolve this, we formally define a Mutational Process (MP) as a unified latent activity that induces coupled mutational signatures across these modalities. We developed MOTET, a Bayesian framework that jointly infers multimodal MPs. Applied to 2,583 whole genomes from the PCAWG cohort, MOTET recovers known MPs more accurately than standard post hoc correlation methods. MOTET also identifies a process linking an SBS37-related signature with a TG>CA-dominated DBS component and resolves canonical SBS12-like activity into two separate MPs with distinct tissue distributions. These results establish a paradigm for formally defining catalogs of MPs and demonstrate that integrating across modalities enhances the ability to discover new mutational patterns.
